@I312256596957@.summary: Lieutenant Samuel Smith was a prominent early settler of New England
@I312256596957@.biography:
📜 Early Life in England
Born: 6 September 1601 (sometimes 1602) in Burstall, near Ipswich, Suffolk, England.
Parents: John Smith (b. 1577, Ipswich) and Mary Gardiner (b. 1575, Elmsett).
Marriage: Married Elizabeth Smythe on 6 October 1624 in Whatfield, Suffolk.
Together they had at least 7 children (5 sons and 2 daughters).

🚢 Migration to New England
Voyage: Samuel Smith sailed from England aboard the Elizabeth of Ipswich in 1634, accompanied by his wife and children.
Early Settlements: Initially lived in Wethersfield, Connecticut, before moving to Hadley, Massachusetts in 1659.

⚔️ Military & Civic Leadership
Held the rank of Lieutenant, overseeing military affairs in Hadley until 1678, when his son Philip succeeded him.
Served as one of the selectmen of Hadley, responsible for local governance and public affairs.
Involved in the founding of Hopkins Grammar School (later Hopkins Academy), one of the earliest endowed schools in Hampshire County.
Registered for military service in 1663 and was active in civic duties well into his 70s.

🪦 Death and Legacy
Died: 17 January 1681 in Hadley, Hampshire County, Massachusetts Bay Colony, aged about 79.
Burial: Old Hadley Cemetery, Hadley, Massachusetts.
Remembered as one of the founding figures of Hadley, with descendants who played important roles in New England history.

@I312413537033@.summary: Mathij (Mathijs) Jansen Van Keuren (also recorded as Van Keulen) was an early Dutch settler in New Netherland, born in the Netherlands in the early 1600s and later emigrating to the Hudson Valley region of colonial New York. He is considered the progenitor of the Van Keuren family in America.
@I312413537033@.biography:
📜 Biographical Overview
Full Name: Mathij (Mathijs) Jansen Van Keuren / Van Keulen
Birth: 2 February 1602, Holland (Reusel-de Mierden, Noord-Brabant, Netherlands)
Parents: Jan Mathijs van Keulen (b. ~1580, Antwerp) and Annetje Jans (b. ~1580)
Marriage: Married Margaret Hendricks in Fort Orange (Albany), New Netherland.
Children:
Jan Matthysen (1638–1724)
Catarina Mattysen Van Keuren (1640–1678)
Annatje Mattesen Jansen Van Keuren (1645–1722)
Matthys Matthysen Van Keuren (1648–1730)

Death: 16 October 1648, New City, Rockland County, New Netherland (present-day New York).

🌍 Historical Context
Dutch Migration: Mathij was part of the wave of Dutch settlers who came to New Netherland in the early 1600s, establishing communities along the Hudson River.
Fort Orange (Albany): His marriage there places him among the earliest families in the Albany area, a key Dutch trading post.
Hudson Valley Settlements: His descendants became prominent in Ulster and Orange Counties, New York, especially in Esopus (Kingston) and Newburgh.

🧬 Family Legacy
The Van Keuren family name (sometimes spelled Van Keulen, VanKeuren, or VanKuelen) traces back to him.
His children and grandchildren spread throughout the Hudson Valley, intermarrying with other early Dutch families such as the DuBois, Van Vliet, and DeWitt families.
The family played roles in colonial conflicts, including the Esopus Wars of the mid-1600s, when Dutch settlers clashed with local Native American groups.
facts: Parents	Jan Mathijs van Keulen & Annetje Jans
Death	16 Oct 1648, Rockland County, New Netherland
Legacy	Founder of Van Keuren family in America

@I312413536740@.summary: Jan Jansen Van Steenbergen (also known as Jan Jansen Van Amersfoort or Timmerman) was a Dutch immigrant born around 1630 in Amersfoort, Utrecht, Netherlands.
@I312413536740@.biography:
📜 Biographical Overview
Birth: ~1630 in Amersfoort, Utrecht, Netherlands.
Parents: Jan Dircksen Van Amersfoort and Fenne Jacobs.
Migration: Sailed as a boy from Amersfoort to New Amsterdam (New York City). By 1658, he was living in Esopus (later Kingston, NY).
Occupation: Known as “Timmerman” (the carpenter), he helped build the stockade at Wiltwijck (Kingston) in 1658.
Marriage: Married Catharyn Mattysen (Van Ceulen) on 3 October 1660 in Wildwyck (Kingston), New Netherland.
Children: Had several children, including Styntje, Thoomes, Gertjen, Sara, and Mateys Van Steenbergh.
Death: Around 1678 in Kingston, Ulster County, New York, aged about 43.

🌍 Historical Context
Esopus Settlement: Jan was among the earliest residents of Esopus (Kingston). In 1658, he signed the agreement to concentrate scattered settlers and erect a protective stockade against Native American attacks.
Name Variants: He was originally styled Jan Jansen Van Amersfoort or Timmerman, but after marriage adopted the surname Van Steenbergh/Van Steenbergen, meaning “of the stone town.”
Legacy: His descendants became part of the Dutch colonial families in Ulster County, intermarrying with other settlers and contributing to the growth of Kingston and surrounding Hudson Valley communities.
facts: Parents	Jan Dircksen Van Amersfoort & Fenne Jacobs
Migration	To New Amsterdam, then Esopus (Kingston) by 1658
Occupation	Carpenter (“Timmerman”), helped build Kingston stockade
Children	Styntje, Thoomes, Gertjen, Sara, Mateys
Legacy	Founder of Van Steenbergh/Van Steenbergen family in New York

@I310088497158@.summary: Medieval knight of the Bacon family, born in 1214 in Baconsthorpe, Norfolk, England
@I310088497158@.biography:
📜 Biographical Overview
Birth: 1214, Baconsthorpe (Thorpe), Norfolk, England.
Parents: Ralph Renoff (or FitzGrimbaldus) de Bacon (b. ~1190) and Damas of Thorpe.
Grandfather: Ranulf de Bacon (b. ~1160), part of the early Bacon line in Norfolk.
Marriage: Married Mary Ann de Ingham in 1239 at Thorpe, Norfolk.
Children: At least one son, Robert Bacon (1245–1290).
Death: 11 June 1294 (some records say 21 June), in Baconsthorpe, Norfolk, aged about 80.
Burial: Baconsthorpe, Norfolk, England.

🏰 Historical Context
The Bacon family was a well‑established gentry line in Norfolk, with roots going back to the Norman period.
Baconsthorpe itself became closely associated with the family name, later the site of Baconsthorpe Castle (built in the 15th century by descendants).
Families like the Bacons were part of the local knightly class, serving in feudal obligations and managing estates.

⚖️ Name Variants & Records
He is sometimes listed as Robert Kimber Bacon or Roger Kimber Bacon, reflecting medieval naming inconsistencies.
The “Kimber” element may have been a descriptive or locational epithet, later incorporated into genealogical records.
Sources differ slightly on dates of death (11 June vs. 21 June 1294), but all agree he lived to about 80 years old.
facts: Parents	Ralph Renoff de Bacon & Damas of Thorpe

@I310088498062@.summary: Grimbald Bacon is remembered as an early Norman ancestor of the Bacon family in Norfolk, born around 1075 in Normandy, but his life details are largely genealogical tradition rather than documented history
@I310088498062@.biography:
📜 Biographical Tradition
Name: Grimbald (Grimbaldus) Bacon
Birth: Around 1075, in Normandy, France (often cited as “Normandie”).
Context: This places him in the generation immediately after the Norman Conquest of England (1066). Many Norman families established themselves in East Anglia during this period.
Lineage: Genealogical accounts often list him as an ancestor of the Bacon family of Baconsthorpe, Norfolk.
Death: Some records suggest he died in Norfolk, England, but exact dates are not preserved.

🏰 Historical Context
After 1066, William the Conqueror rewarded Norman knights and followers with lands in England. Families like the Bacons are thought to have come over during this wave.
The name “Bacon” itself may derive from a place-name in Normandy (such as Bacquepuis or Bacquerville), or from descriptive origins.
Grimbald is often cited as one of the founders of the Bacon line in England, though hard evidence is lacking.

⚖️ Notes on Sources
Most references to Grimbald Bacon come from later genealogical compilations (16th–19th century antiquarians) rather than contemporary medieval charters.
He is sometimes listed as the father or grandfather of Ranulf de Bacon (b. ~1160), who appears more clearly in Norfolk records.
Because of the scarcity of medieval documentation, Grimbald’s existence is best treated as semi-legendary—a traditional ancestor figure rather than a fully documented knight.
facts: Migration	To England after Norman Conquest
Role	Traditional progenitor of Bacon family in Norfolk
Legacy	Ancestor of Ranulf de Bacon and later Baconsthorpe line

@I310088492223@.summary: Sir Michael Bacon of Suffolk was a Tudor-era gentleman whose family line remained influential in East Anglia
@I310088492223@.biography:
Sir Michael Bacon was born in 1535 in Suffolk, England, and lived until 1614/1615. He was part of the Bacon family of Helmingham and Winston, Suffolk, married Elizabeth Wylie in 1565, and had a large family whose descendants carried the Bacon name into later centuries.

📜 Biographical Overview
Birth: 31 March 1535, Winston/Helmingham, Suffolk, England.
Parents: John Bacon (b. ~1505, d. 1558) and Margaret Hall (or Margaret Unknown, depending on source).
Grandparents: Thomas Bacon (b. ~1475) and Joan Unknown.
Marriage: Married Elizabeth Wylie on 16 August 1565 in Helmingham, Suffolk.
Children: At least 10 children, including:
John Bacon (1566–1615)
Joanna Bacon (1567–1614)
Mary Bacon (1569–1646)
Sir Thomas Bacon (1572–1615)
Susanna Bacon (1574–1664)
William Bacon (1577–1653)
Michael Bacon (1579–1648)
Rose Bacon (1582–1614)
Sarah Bacon (1584–1614)
Elizabeth Bacon (dates uncertain)
Death: 25 March 1615 (some records say before October 1614), Winston, Suffolk, aged about 79.
Burial: St. Andrew’s Churchyard, Winston, Suffolk.

🏰 Historical Context
The Bacon family of Suffolk was a prominent gentry line, with branches connected to Helmingham and later to Baconsthorpe in Norfolk.
Michael lived during the Tudor period, spanning the reigns of Henry VIII, Edward VI, Mary I, and Elizabeth I.
His lifetime overlapped with the rise of Sir Nicholas Bacon (1510–1579), Lord Keeper of the Great Seal, and Francis Bacon (1561–1626), the philosopher and statesman. While Michael belonged to another branch of the family, these connections highlight the Bacon family’s broad influence in East Anglia.
facts: Children	10 (John, Joanna, Mary, Thomas, Susanna, William, Michael, Rose, Sarah, Elizabeth)
Death	25 Mar 1615 (or before Oct 1614), Winston, Suffolk

Slovakia.biography:
🇸🇰 Slovakia in the 19th Century

Political Context
- Slovakia was part of the Kingdom of Hungary within the Austro-Hungarian Empire.
- Slovaks faced Magyarization policies—suppression of their language, schools, and cultural identity.
- Limited political rights and representation fueled frustration.

Economic Conditions
- Predominantly agrarian society: most Slovaks were peasants farming small plots.
- Land shortages and inheritance customs left younger generations with little or no land.
- Frequent crop failures and famines (especially in the 1840s and 1870s).
- Cottage industries (weaving, mining) declined as industrialization bypassed rural Slovakia.

Social & Cultural Life
- Strong Catholic and Lutheran traditions shaped village life.
- Folk customs, music, and festivals were central to identity.
- Education was limited, especially in Slovak language schools, which were often closed by Hungarian authorities.

🌍 Why Slovaks Emigrated

Push Factors (Leaving Slovakia)
- Poverty and unemployment due to agricultural decline.
- Political oppression under Hungarian rule.
- Military conscription in the Austro-Hungarian army.
- Population pressure: too many people for too little land.

Pull Factors (Coming to Binghamton)
- Industrial jobs: Binghamton was booming with cigar manufacturing, shoe factories, and later other industries.
- Higher wages compared to subsistence farming in Slovakia.
- Chain migration: Slovaks followed relatives or neighbors who had already settled.
- Religious freedom: Ability to worship without state interference.
- Community support: Ethnic parishes and fraternal organizations provided social safety nets.

🏭 Binghamton as a Destination
By the late 19th century, Binghamton was known as the “Valley of Opportunity” because of its factories and industries. Slovaks found work in cigar factories, shoe manufacturing plants, and construction. They established Catholic parishes, fraternal lodges, and ethnic clubs, which became centers of community life. Slovaks often lived in ethnic neighborhoods, preserving traditions while adapting to American society.

Netherlands-B.summary: Between 1610 and 1650, the Netherlands experienced its peak Golden Age, marked by global trade dominance, flourishing art, and political consolidation under the Dutch Republic.
Netherlands-B.biography:
📜 Political Landscape
Dutch Republic: Formed from the Union of Utrecht (1579), the Seven Provinces operated as a confederation with significant autonomy.

Twelve Years’ Truce (1609–1621): A temporary halt in the Eighty Years’ War against Spain, allowing the Dutch to focus on trade and expansion.

Resumption of War (1621–1648): Hostilities with Spain resumed until the Treaty of Münster (1648), part of the Peace of Westphalia, which formally recognized Dutch independence.

Internal Struggles: Tensions between the republican States Party and the House of Orange (stadtholders) shaped politics, especially during wartime.

🌍 Economic and Global Expansion
Dutch East India Company (VOC, founded 1602): Expanded aggressively in Asia, controlling spice trade routes and establishing Batavia (Jakarta) as its headquarters.

Dutch West India Company (WIC, founded 1621): Focused on the Americas and Africa, including Brazil and the Caribbean, and played a major role in the Atlantic slave trade.

Amsterdam: Became the financial capital of Europe, with the Amsterdam Stock Exchange (1602) and advanced banking systems.

Maritime Power: Dutch fleets dominated global shipping, often referred to as the “carriers of Europe.”

🎨 Cultural Flourishing
Art: The Dutch Golden Age produced iconic painters:

Rembrandt van Rijn (1606–1669): Known for works like The Night Watch (1642).

Johannes Vermeer (1632–1675): Specialized in intimate domestic scenes.

Frans Hals and Jacob van Ruisdael: Masters of portraiture and landscapes.

Science & Philosophy:

René Descartes lived in the Netherlands during the 1620s–1640s, publishing Meditations (1641).

Advances in optics, cartography, and engineering reflected Dutch innovation.

⚔️ Military and Diplomacy
Naval Conflicts: The Dutch fought England in the Anglo-Dutch Wars (first beginning in 1652).

Peace of Westphalia (1648): Ended the Thirty Years’ War in Europe and secured Dutch independence, cementing their role as a major European power.

@I310053590537@.summary: Frans Jacobson (Jacobszen) Van Oudewater was a Dutch settler born around 1632 in Oudewater, Utrecht, Netherlands, who emigrated to New Netherland and died in New York around 1665–1666. He is recognized as one of the early colonists whose descendants became part of the Dutch-American community in New York and New Jersey.
@I310053590537@.biography:
📜 Key Biographical Details
Name Variants: Frans Jacobson Van Oudewater, Jacobszen Oudewater, Outwater, Jacobsen.

Birth: About 1632–1635, in Oudewater, Utrecht, Netherlands.

Migration: He emigrated to New Netherland (present-day New York) in the mid-17th century. Some records suggest he arrived aboard De Bever in 1661.

Marriage: Married Geertruid (Geertje) Gerrits before 1652 in the Netherlands.

Children:

Maria Franse Oudewater

Thomas Fransen Oudewater (ca. 1661–1753), who carried on the family line in New York.

Death: Around 1665–1666, in Nieuw-Nederland (New York).

🏛 Historical Context
New Netherland Colony: By the time Frans arrived, New Amsterdam (Manhattan) and Fort Orange (Albany) were thriving Dutch settlements.

Dutch Families: His family was part of the wave of Dutch immigrants who established roots in the Hudson Valley and Bergen County, NJ.

Legacy: His descendants, especially through Thomas Fransen Oudewater, became integrated into Dutch-American society, with later generations adopting Anglicized surnames like Outwater.
facts: Name Variants	Van Oudewater, Jacobszen, Outwater
Migration	To New Netherland, possibly on De Bever (1661)

@I312048921475@.biography:
The original American of the Haven lineage was Richard Haven, who was born in west England
in 1620. He and his wife, Susanna Newhall, were of Puritan stock, having immigrated to America as newlyweds in 1645, about twenty years after the Mayflower, and settled in Lynn, Massachusetts.
Richard and Susanna arrived in America, not as indentured servants in bondage, to the shipping
companies in payment of their passage, but as freemen. Richard served under Captain Samuel
Brocklebank in the King Phillip's War as a Sergeant. They were part of the Separatist movement that peopled Massachusetts and other colonies with settlers who valued their religion and worked hard to establish farms and homes in this land, where they were free to practice the religion they chose. Six generations of Havens made Massachusetts their home.
